topics: 🔤 Five Cases That Look Like 'God Alone Knows' — But Aren't — testing Yom Kippur's atonement against five uncertain-purification cases
📜 Three Verses of 'Knowing' — the elimination process proving a sin offering is still owed even after Yom Kippur
🛡️ What Does a Provisional Guilt Offering Actually Accomplish? — Rabbi Zeira and Rava on its true purpose
🐦 Can the Uncertain Bird Offering Be Eaten? — Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute a delicate timing question
🐏 Two Rams for Two Sela — a new mishna on tracking value across a guilt offering and its misuse payment

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Limits of 'A Sin Only God Knows'
overview.subtitle: Keritot 26a–26b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf tests the principle that Yom Kippur atones only for 'a sin known only to God' against five cases that seem to fit that description just as well — a woman uncertain if her miscarriage requires an offering, an uncertain leper, an uncertain nazirite, a suspected sotah, and the decapitated heifer — showing each time why the case is really different. It then works through a rigorous three-way elimination proving that all three Torah mentions of 'when it becomes known to him' are needed, ultimately teaching that a sin offering is still owed even after Yom Kippur passes. After exploring what a provisional guilt offering actually accomplishes if a sin offering is needed anyway, the daf turns to a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan over whether an uncertain bird sin offering may be eaten once certainty arrives after its neck is already pinched, and closes with a new mishna tracking value shifts across paired rams purchased for a guilt offering and its associated misuse payment.

callout.label: The recurring move:
callout.text: Every apparent counterexample is defused by showing the case either isn't truly 'unknown to everyone,' or the offering in question was never about atonement to begin with.

slides.title: 📜 Three Verses of 'Knowing' — The Elimination Process
slides.subtitle: Why does the Torah repeat 'when it becomes known to him' three separate times?

steps.content: 1️⃣ The phrase appears for an individual's sin offering, a Nasi's, and the community's (Lev. 4:14, 23, 28) — could any one be derived from the others?
2️⃣ Individual from Nasi? No — a Nasi is uniquely exempt from the 'hearing a voice' oath category; individuals aren't
3️⃣ Community from Nasi? No — a Nasi's offerings sometimes include a female animal; the community's never does
4️⃣ Every combination of 'derive two from one' fails the same way — each category has some unique feature blocking the derivation

5️⃣ Conclusion: since none is truly extra for its own halakha, the 'leftover' teaching applies elsewhere — that a sin offering is required even when the sin becomes known only AFTER Yom Kippur has passed

callout.label: Abaye's version:
callout.text: Abaye reaches the same conclusion through a different verbal analogy ('mitzvot'/'mitzvot' linking all three sin-offering categories), showing multiple paths lead to the same halakha.

slides.title: 🛡️ What Does a Provisional Guilt Offering Actually Accomplish?
slides.subtitle: If a sin offering is still needed once certainty arrives, what was the point of the earlier offering?

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: Rava derives from 'if his sin becomes known to him' (Lev. 4:28) that a sin offering is owed whenever certainty eventually arrives — even after a provisional guilt offering was already brought. So what did that earlier offering actually achieve?

lines.speaker: Rabbi Zeira
lines.text: It matters in case he dies before learning the truth — then at least he dies without that iniquity counted against him.

lines.speaker: Rava's objection
lines.text: That can't be the reason — death itself already absolves a person of sin! No special offering is needed for that.

lines.speaker: Rava's real answer
lines.text: Its true purpose is to protect the person from the anguish and suffering of living under unresolved guilt while awaiting clarity — the Torah spares the person's peace of mind, not his ultimate legal record.

callout.label: Reframing the offering:
callout.text: A provisional guilt offering isn't really about final atonement — it is about immediate psychological and spiritual relief during genuine uncertainty.

slides.title: 🐦 Can the Uncertain Bird Offering Be Eaten?
slides.subtitle: Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute what happens when certainty arrives just after pinching

boxes.title: Rav: yes, it may be eaten
items: Once the blood is sprinkled/squeezed after pinching, atonement is achieved regardless of what's later confirmed
A supporting baraita (Levi) explicitly permits eating in this case

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan: no, it's still forbidden
items: A rabbinic decree — permitting it risks people mistakenly thinking ANY uncertain bird offering may be eaten, even in ordinary unresolved cases
A supporting baraita explicitly forbids eating, even forbidding BENEFIT once blood is fully processed

callout.label: Underlying principle either way:
callout.text: Both agree the sprinkling accomplishes genuine atonement (fulfilling the woman's purification) — they disagree only on whether a protective rabbinic fence should still bar consumption.

slides.title: 🐏 Two Rams for Two Sela
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: tracking value shifts when two rams are purchased with guilt-offering funds

lines.speaker: The scenario
lines.text: Someone sets aside two sela for a guilt offering and buys TWO rams instead of one — misusing consecrated funds. One ram is now worth two sela; the other, ten dinars (2.5 sela). Which offering does which ram serve?

lines.speaker: Gemara's question
lines.text: What does 'the second ram covers his misuse' (מְעִילָתוֹ) actually mean — the misuse GUILT OFFERING itself, or merely the REPAYMENT (principal plus a fifth) for the stolen value?

lines.speaker: First reading challenged
lines.text: If 'misuse' meant the guilt-offering ram itself, that would mean the added one-fifth payment comes bundled WITH the ram — but the Torah (Lev. 5:16) clearly requires the one-fifth to accompany the STOLEN VALUE repayment, not the offering animal!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: So 'his misuse' in the first clause must mean the REPAYMENT for what he stole — yet the mishna's LATER clause seems to use 'misuse' to mean the guilt-offering ram itself, creating an internal inconsistency the Gemara must still resolve.

callout.label: Ongoing puzzle:
callout.text: The mishna's own two clauses appear to use the identical term 'me'ilato' in two different senses — a tension the Gemara continues untangling into the next daf.

summary.principle: Yom Kippur's atonement for 'a sin known only to God' is narrower than it first appears — excluding purification-focused offerings and cases where someone besides the sinner knows the truth — while a provisional guilt offering serves immediate relief rather than final atonement, and precise terminology in the mishna's rulings must be carefully disambiguated rather than assumed.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, why does Yom Kippur NOT exempt a woman with an uncertain miscarriage from bringing her sin offering afterward, despite this seeming to be 'a sin known only to God'?
o: Because women are never included in Yom Kippur's atonement
Because her offering is brought for purification (to permit eating sacrificial food), not for atonement — Yom Kippur atones for 'all their sins' but not 'all their impurity'
Because miscarriage is always a definite, known event
Because Yom Kippur only atones for men
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes her offering as serving a purification function rather than an atonement function, and Yom Kippur's atonement covers sins specifically, not impurity-related purification requirements.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's elimination process regarding the three 'knowing' verses (individual, Nasi, community sin offerings), why can't the individual's requirement be derived from the Nasi's?
o: Because individuals never bring sin offerings
Because a Nasi is uniquely exempt from the sin offering for the 'hearing a voice' oath category, while individuals are not exempt from it
Because Nasi offerings are always more expensive
Because there is no difference between them at all
quiz.e: The Gemara shows that a Nasi's sin offering obligations are more lenient in that a Nasi is excluded from the 'hearing a voice' oath's sin offering, a leniency that doesn't apply to an individual, blocking direct derivation.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final explanation, what is the actual purpose of bringing a provisional guilt offering, if a sin offering is still required once the sin becomes definitively known?
o: It has no purpose at all
It protects the person from suffering and anguish during the period of genuine uncertainty, not final atonement
It replaces the need for a sin offering entirely
It is required only for financial reasons
quiz.e: Rava concludes that the provisional guilt offering's function is to spare the person from ongoing suffering while the uncertainty remains unresolved, since a sin offering is still ultimately required once the sin is confirmed.

quiz.q: What is the core disagreement between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding an uncertain bird sin offering when certainty of birth arrives after the bird's neck has already been pinched?
o: Whether the bird achieves any atonement at all
Whether the meat may be eaten afterward — Rav permits it since atonement was achieved, while Rabbi Yoḥanan forbids it as a rabbinic decree to prevent confusion with ordinary uncertain offerings
Whether the bird must be a specific species
Whether the woman must bring a second bird
quiz.e: Both agree the sprinkling achieves genuine atonement/purification, but they disagree on eating the meat: Rav permits it, while Rabbi Yoḥanan prohibits it as a protective rabbinic decree against people mistakenly eating ordinary unresolved uncertain bird offerings.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's challenge in the new mishna, why can't 'his misuse' (me'ilato) in the mishna's first clause refer to the guilt-offering ram itself?
o: Because guilt offerings are never made from rams
Because the Torah (Leviticus 5:16) requires the added one-fifth payment to accompany the repayment for the STOLEN value, not the offering animal itself
Because the mishna never mentions any payment at all
Because rams cannot be valued in sela
quiz.e: The Gemara demonstrates that if 'his misuse' referred to the guilt-offering animal, it would wrongly imply the one-fifth payment travels with the offering animal, contradicting the Torah's requirement that the one-fifth accompanies the restitution for the stolen value itself.
